extracted.intended_audience: economists, political economists, and social scientists studying persuasion, media, financial markets, and information economics (graduate students, researchers, policy analysts).
extracted.subtask_description: A scholarly review of empirical and theoretical models of persuasive communication across markets (advertising, financial analysts, media, political persuasion), analyzing when messages affect beliefs or preferences and the incentives of senders. Focuses on mechanisms (belief-based vs preference-based), attention/endogenous exposure, and supply-side incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-earnings announcement drift
rubrics_metrics.description: Companies that release positive (negative) earnings news experience continuous increases (decreases) in stock prices over the next 2–4 quarters; predictable stock returns persist instead of being arbitraged away.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes an empirical regularity puzzling for efficient markets; used as evidence that market participants underreact or attention is limited. Studies document slow initial incorporation and subsequent drift in returns following earnings announcements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyst information types
rubrics_metrics.description: Analysts provide three observable types of information: (i) stock recommendations (Strong Buy/Buy/Hold/Sell/Strong Sell), (ii) earnings forecasts (e.g., expected profit per share for upcoming quarter), and (iii) long-term growth estimates (e.g., percent growth per year).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These signals are publicly observed soon after release and closely monitored by investors; each type has different verifiability and potential for bias. Empirical analyses use these categories to measure analyst influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Belief-based models of persuasion
rubrics_metrics.description: Persuasion works by changing receivers' beliefs. This includes fully Bayesian informative/signalling models and non-Bayesian models of limited memory, categorical thinking, or neglect of sender incentives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Core empirical predictions include: larger effects when receivers are less certain; inferences depend on sender credibility; increasing information supply tends to improve welfare under rational receivers. Evidence: advertising more effective for inexperienced consumers; endorsements matter when surprising.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference-based models of persuasion
rubrics_metrics.description: Persuasion affects behavior independently of beliefs by entering the receiver's utility (e.g., advertising altering preferences) or via peripheral, non-informational psychological factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Predicts that non-informational message content (imagery, attractiveness, framing) can have behavioral effects even if it conveys no factual information. Also can explain costly avoidance of persuasive messages. Empirical examples include ad content manipulations and attractiveness effects in fundraising.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effectiveness increases with receiver uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Persuasion tends to be more effective when receivers have weaker priors or less experience with the product/politics, so new information has a larger impact on beliefs and behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical support: Ackerberg (yogurt ads) — inexperienced buyers respond more to ads; political evidence shows less-updated views among highly aware voters. Use interaction analyses between exposure and prior knowledge/experience to test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sender credibility conditions inference weight
rubrics_metrics.description: Receivers' inferences from a message depend on beliefs about the sender's credibility; surprising endorsements from typically-opposed sources carry more weight than routine endorsements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bayesian prediction: institutional/sophisticated receivers adjust for credibility more than inexperienced ones. Empirical examples: newspaper endorsements that are a 'surprise' have larger voting effects; analyst recommendation reforms altered informativeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sophistication heterogeneity in receiver response
rubrics_metrics.description: Sophisticated (institutional) agents adjust for sender incentives and credibility, while inexperienced/individual agents under-adjust and take optimistic/distorted signals at face value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence: institutional investors respond differently to affiliated analysts' recommendations than individual investors; sophisticated traders may trade against biased signals that individual investors follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-informational content can causally affect behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Features of messages that do not convey verifiable information—imagery, attractiveness, narrative, framing—can produce economically significant behavioral changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ad slogans with no product-relevant truth, marketing imagery varying with market conditions, randomized mailer content affecting loan takeup. Empirical tests randomize content (images, examples, suggested uses) and compare takeup impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Receivers may engage in costly avoidance of persuasion
rubrics_metrics.description: Agents sometimes take costly steps (e.g., not being home, crossing the street) to avoid exposure to persuasive solicitations, suggesting persuasion can have direct utility effects beyond information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication favors preference-based mechanisms; demonstrated in field experiments on door-to-door fundraising where advance notifications reduce exposure and donations substantially.

rubrics_metrics.name: Endogenous exposure and limited attention affect persuasion
rubrics_metrics.description: Persuasion is only effective when messages are actually received; receivers choose what information to seek and how to allocate attention, leading to underreaction when attention is limited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical signatures: slower immediate incorporation of earnings news on low-attention days (Fridays, days with many announcements) and larger subsequent drift. Implication: timing and salience matter; selection into exposure must be addressed in identification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demand for ideologically consistent news (audience slant)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consumers display demand for news that aligns with their political beliefs, which shapes the overall effect of persuasive messages and the supply of slanted content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical approach: measure slant of newspapers and estimate demand and supply; findings suggest consumer demand largely explains average slant in US newspapers. Implication: effects of persuasion depend on sorting and selective exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tradeoff between distortion and reputation in senders' incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Senders balance incentives to distort information to influence receivers against incentives to build reputation for accuracy (if receivers are rational, reputation can limit distortion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This balance varies across markets: monopoly senders may distort more; competitive media may invest in credibility. Theoretical implication for welfare: more information supply improves welfare in rational belief-based settings but may harm welfare when persuasion changes preferences or receivers are non-Bayesian.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertisers' incentives and scope for cheap talk
rubrics_metrics.description: Firms advertising to sell products may not internalize accuracy; communication can be pure cheap talk, and advertising can affect preferences directly rather than convey credible information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulation, verifiable claims, and reputation can limit distortion. Empirical investigations include analysis of unverifiable claims and the inconsistent effects of advertising across contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevalence of unsupported claims in pharmaceutical advertising
rubrics_metrics.description: A substantial share of pharmaceutical ads in medical journals contain claims not supported by the cited studies (evidence: ~44% unsupported in one study).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as an empirical example of advertiser distortion; suggests the need for external verification and scrutiny in domains with high consequences for misrepresentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of third-party certifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective third parties (certifiers, report cards, ratings) can provide credible information that mitigates distortions and significantly affect consumer behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: restaurant health scores increasing attendance to high-rated restaurants and lowering food poisoning incidents; rankings and product ratings influence choices. Policy implication: certifiers can correct market failures due to biased senders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incentives for firms to manipulate financial reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Firms have incentives to manage reported earnings (within GAAP/'street' frameworks) to meet analyst forecasts or portray more favorable results, despite regulatory constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical indicators: bunching at analyst consensus (DeGeorge et al.), associations between proxies for accounting management and subsequent negative returns, and prominence given to the more favorable earnings measure in press releases (GAAP vs pro-forma).

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyst career incentives favor optimism over accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Promotions and career movements for analysts are more strongly associated with optimism (positive bias) than with forecast accuracy; optimism increases promotion probability more than accuracy does.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence: analysts with top optimism scores have much higher promotion likelihoods than equally accurate analysts. Implication: career incentives can generate systematic upward bias in forecasts and recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affiliated analysts exhibit stronger buy-bias and are less informative
rubrics_metrics.description: Analysts affiliated with brokerage/investment banks (with corporate finance incentives) issue far more Buy/Strong Buy recommendations (over 70%) and fewer Sell recommendations, producing biased distributions that reduce informativeness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: investors should discount affiliated analysts; institutional investors appear to do so while retail investors do not. Empirical distributions show skew toward Buy recommendations; affiliation intensifies bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time-varying analyst forecast optimism (the 'walk-down')
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyst forecasts tend to be optimistic at longer horizons, become less optimistic as the release approaches, and sometimes turn pessimistic in the final months before earnings — a pattern described as a 'walk-down'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This pattern may reflect changing incentives as managerial/market pressures evolve near release dates. Historical differences (e.g., 1980s vs 1990s) change the magnitude; trading strategies exploiting this pattern have produced excess returns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competition moderates analyst optimism bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Greater competition among analysts reduces optimism bias in earnings forecasts; reductions in competition (e.g., from mergers) lead remaining analysts to increase optimism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical strategy: use bank mergers as instruments for decreased competition. Findings show increased optimism in forecasts and long-term growth estimates post-merger, suggesting competition restrains bias but does not eliminate it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media firms' incentives driven by audience demand and supply-side factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Media content is shaped both by consumer demand for slant (readers' ideological preferences) and supply-side incentives (owner preferences, advertiser/political pressure, reporter tastes), with evidence that demand often plays the dominant role in average slant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical analyses measure newspaper slant and decompose variance into demand and supply components; case studies (LA Times) show ownership can shift slant. Implication: to evaluate media bias, account for both demand and supply forces and local clustering/ownership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Channel-specific persuasion effectiveness (in-person > phone > mail)
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal, in-person interactions generate larger persuasion effects than phone calls, which in turn are more effective than mailers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical support from get-out-the-vote and fundraising studies (e.g., Gerber and Green). When assessing persuasive campaigns, consider the delivery channel and personal interaction intensity.
